$comment: Industry profiles. Two jobs: (1) supply the vocabulary that fills {slots} in universal questions so they sound native, (2) tell you what earns trust and what makes you sound like a tourist. Read the profile before the interview; use the slots when reading a universal question aloud.

profiles.label: Healthcare & Medicine
profiles.status_axis: Specialty prestige, procedural skill, and how calm you are in a code. Publishing matters in academic settings and almost nowhere else.
profiles.earns_trust: Knowing that documentation and prior authorization eat more of the day than medicine does. Distinguishing what the clinician controls from what the system imposes.
landmines: Asking for a specific patient story without noting that they should keep it de-identified.
Treating 'burnout' as a personal resilience failure rather than a workload and autonomy problem.
Assuming doctors set prices or control billing.

profiles.label: Law
profiles.status_axis: Firm tier and partnership track in private practice; trial record in litigation; clerkships early on. Public-interest lawyers run an entirely different status game.
profiles.earns_trust: Understanding that most litigation never reaches trial and most transactional work is risk allocation, not argument. Knowing privilege limits what they can tell you.
landmines: Asking them to comment on a live matter.
Conflating 'defended someone guilty' with a moral failure - it is the job and they have answered it a thousand times.
Assuming every lawyer goes to court.

profiles.label: Finance & Insurance
profiles.status_axis: P&L attribution and proximity to risk-taking. Being right when consensus was wrong is the currency; being right with consensus counts for little.
profiles.earns_trust: Asking about process rather than picks. Recognizing compliance constraints on what they can say about positions or clients.
landmines: Asking for stock tips or current positioning - it can be a regulatory problem, not just a dodge.
Treating all of finance as one job. A claims adjuster, a quant, and a CFP share almost nothing.
Assuming high pay means the work is easy or the person is unserious.

profiles.label: Technology
profiles.status_axis: Scope of systems owned and technical judgment respected by peers. Titles are noisy across companies and everyone knows it.
profiles.earns_trust: Asking about maintenance, migration, and legacy systems rather than only about the new and shiny.
landmines: Assuming everyone in tech is a startup founder or wants to be.
Asking 'how do I learn to code' as a substitute for a real question.
Treating the last eighteen months of AI news as the whole of the field.

profiles.label: Manufacturing
profiles.status_axis: Being the person who can actually fix the machine. Tenure on a specific line is real authority regardless of title.
profiles.earns_trust: Knowing that yield, takt time, and scrap are the daily scoreboard, and that a plant runs on relationships between the floor and the office.
landmines: Nostalgia framing - treating manufacturing as a museum piece rather than a live, automated, technical field.
Assuming offshoring is a simple cost decision.
Talking to a plant manager as if they set the product roadmap.

profiles.label: Skilled Trades & Construction
profiles.status_axis: Clean work that holds up, and the ability to solve a problem nobody else on site can. License level and years in matter; formal education does not.
profiles.earns_trust: Asking about the parts of the job that are diagnosis rather than labor. Acknowledging the body cost and the business side of running a small shop.
landmines: Framing the trades as a fallback for people who could not do college.
Assuming the work is unskilled repetition rather than constant improvisation against old buildings.
Asking for free advice about your own house instead of asking about their work.

profiles.label: Agriculture & Food Production
profiles.status_axis: Land stewardship over generations, and yields nobody had to bail you out for. Debt discipline is quietly the whole game.
profiles.earns_trust: Understanding that they are price takers, not price setters, and that weather, commodity markets, and input costs are three separate risks.
landmines: Casual moralizing about industrial versus organic without knowing their economics.
Assuming farming is low-technology.
Treating subsidies as a handout without asking how the program actually works.

profiles.label: Education
profiles.status_axis: Respect from other teachers, which is earned by classroom management and results with hard students - not by administration's metrics.
profiles.earns_trust: Distinguishing the teaching from the paperwork, the policy, and the parenting the job now absorbs.
landmines: 'Those who can't do, teach' energy in any form.
Assuming test scores measure the thing they care about.
Asking a teacher to speak for all of education policy.

profiles.label: Hospitality & Food Service
profiles.status_axis: Consistency under volume. Anyone can cook one great plate; running four hundred covers without a miss is the flex.
profiles.earns_trust: Knowing the margins are thin, the labor math is brutal, and the romantic chef narrative is mostly a media product.
landmines: Asking about their 'passion for food' as an opener - it is the most exhausted question in the industry.
Ignoring the back-of-house, or ignoring the front-of-house.
Assuming a full restaurant means a profitable one.

profiles.label: Logistics & Supply Chain
profiles.status_axis: Knowing where the real constraint is before anyone else does, and having the relationships to get capacity when there is none.
profiles.earns_trust: Understanding that the job is exception handling, not planning, and that most of the system runs on phone calls and trust.
landmines: Assuming 2020-21 was the first time supply chains were hard.
Treating drivers as interchangeable labor when talking to anyone who has driven.
Believing software solved this.

profiles.label: Energy & Utilities
profiles.status_axis: Safety record and reliability. In this field, an uneventful career is the mark of excellence, which is hard to talk about on a podcast.
profiles.earns_trust: Separating the engineering from the politics. Knowing that regulated utilities cannot simply choose what to build.
landmines: Asking someone to defend or attack their entire sector as a proxy for climate politics.
Assuming the grid is a single thing rather than interconnections, markets, and regulators.
Underestimating how much of the job is permitting.

profiles.label: Creative Arts
profiles.status_axis: Peer respect and the ability to keep making work. Commercial success is real but sits uneasily next to it.
profiles.earns_trust: Asking about process and revision rather than inspiration. Taking the business side seriously - rights, royalties, and who owns what.
landmines: 'Where do you get your ideas' in any phrasing.
Assuming they can live on the art alone, or assuming they cannot.
Asking them to explain the meaning of a specific work as if there is an answer key.

profiles.label: Media & Journalism
profiles.status_axis: Scoops and sourcing. Being first and right. Beat expertise ages into authority.
profiles.earns_trust: Understanding sourcing rules and why they will not burn one. Knowing the business model collapse is not an abstraction to them.
landmines: Asking them to reveal a source, even hypothetically.
Treating 'the media' as a monolith with a single agenda.
Assuming reporters write their own headlines.

profiles.label: Nonprofit & Social Impact

vocabulary.bad_outcome: a program that did not move the needle

profiles.status_axis: Proximity to the actual work versus proximity to the money - and the tension between the two is a live wire worth pulling.
profiles.earns_trust: Knowing that funder priorities distort programs, and that overhead ratios are a bad metric everyone is forced to perform.
landmines: Assuming low pay means the work is not professionalized.
Framing beneficiaries as passive recipients.
Treating impact measurement as simple.

profiles.label: Public Sector & Government
profiles.status_axis: Institutional memory and the ability to make the machine actually move. Career staff quietly outlast appointees and know it.
profiles.earns_trust: Understanding that constraints are statutory, not chosen, and that 'why don't you just' has an answer that is usually a law.
landmines: Lazy bureaucrat framing.
Asking a civil servant to comment on elected officials or partisan politics - many genuinely cannot.
Assuming they have discretion they do not have.

profiles.label: Retail & E-commerce
profiles.status_axis: A buyer's instinct that turns into sell-through. In stores, the manager who can run a holiday weekend without drama.
profiles.earns_trust: Knowing inventory is the whole business - cash converted into guesses about the future - and that returns and shrink quietly eat margin.
landmines: Retail apocalypse framing.
Assuming store work is unskilled.
Talking about brand while ignoring unit economics, or the reverse.

profiles.label: Real Estate & Development

vocabulary.bad_outcome: a deal that dies at closing

profiles.status_axis: Deals closed and capital raised. In development, what you have actually built and whether it still stands up.
profiles.earns_trust: Knowing that entitlement and financing take longer than construction, and that most of the work is managing a chain of people who can each kill the deal.
landmines: Treating agents as glorified door openers.
Assuming developers control zoning or timelines.
Asking for market predictions as the main event.

profiles.label: Science & Research

vocabulary.bad_outcome: a result that will not replicate

profiles.status_axis: Publication venue and citation, plus a quieter reputation for whose data holds up. Grant funding is survival and everyone knows the ratio.
profiles.earns_trust: Understanding that most of research is failed experiments and grant writing, and that the incentive structure is a known and painful topic.
landmines: Asking for certainty they will not give.
Treating one preprint as settled science.
Assuming a PI still does bench work.

profiles.label: Sports & Athletics
profiles.status_axis: Performance under scrutiny, and the locker-room read on whether you are a pro. Contracts are public and that shapes everything.
profiles.earns_trust: Asking about preparation, film, and the boring repetition rather than only the highlight. Taking the labor and business side seriously.
landmines: Asking an athlete to relive a career-defining failure without warning.
Treating the body as a machine and ignoring the career-length anxiety.
Assuming coaches control roster decisions.

profiles.label: Defense & Military
profiles.status_axis: Competence under load and what you did for the people next to you. Rank is formal authority; reputation in the unit is the real one.
profiles.earns_trust: Knowing the difference between what is classified, what is sensitive, and what is simply not yours to ask. Asking about the job, not the war stories.
landmines: 'Did you ever kill anyone.' Never.
Thank-you-for-your-service framing as a substitute for a real question.
Assuming combat arms is the whole military - most of it is logistics, maintenance, and administration.

profiles.label: Actuarial Science
profiles.status_axis: Credentials first - the exam track is long, public, and the visible currency for a decade. After that it is whose numbers hold up under audit and regulatory review, and who is willing to sign the opinion.
profiles.earns_trust: Knowing the hard part is setting assumptions rather than doing the math, that most of the work is data cleaning and model maintenance, and that an actuary does not set prices - regulators, competition and the business all bound the answer.
landmines: Confusing them with accountants or with quants. All three touch numbers and share almost nothing else.
Asking them to predict a specific event. They price distributions, not outcomes, and the difference is the whole profession.
Assuming they set prices. They produce an indicated rate; what gets filed and sold is someone else's decision.
Treating the exams as trivia. It is years of unpaid evenings and it is how the field decides who you are.

$slots_note: Slot values are bare singular nouns so they can be dropped into sentences like 'a {work_unit}' or 'your {customer}'. Articles come from the question text; fill_slots() corrects a/an automatically. Richer secondary terms live in also_called and are for your own preparation, not for substitution.
